title: What an ORM is (and isn't)
summary: Objects in your program, rows in a table, and the library that translates between them.

steps.title: Two worlds
body: Your C# program thinks in **objects**: a `Book` with a `Title` and a `Year`, a list of books, a reference from a book to its author.
A relational database thinks in **tables**: a `Books` table with a row per book and a column per field, and a number in one row that points at a row in another table.
| C# | Database |
| class `Book` | table `Books` |
| an object | a row |
| a property | a column |
| a reference to an `Author` | a foreign key column `AuthorId` |
| a LINQ query | a SQL `SELECT` |
Without help, you translate by hand: write SQL as strings, run it, read each column of each row, and copy it into objects. Every query, every insert, every update.

An **ORM** (object-relational mapper) does that translation for you. **Entity Framework Core** (EF Core) is the ORM that ships with .NET. You describe your classes once; EF Core writes the SQL, runs it, and turns the rows back into objects.

steps.prompt: Which of these does an ORM like EF Core do for you?
options: Turns a LINQ query over `Books` into a SQL `SELECT`, and the rows it returns into `Book` objects
Makes a badly designed database fast without any thought from you
Removes the need for a database server or file
Guarantees that two users can never overwrite each other's changes
steps.explain: EF Core translates. It does not design your schema, choose your indexes, or settle conflicts between users on its own. Those are still your decisions, and later modules show how to express them.

steps.prompt: Sort each job: does EF Core do it for you, or is it still your job?
items: Writing the `INSERT` statement for a new object
Choosing which columns need an index
Avoiding one query per item in a loop
Deciding what happens when two people edit the same row
steps.explain: EF Core removes the boring, error-prone translation work. Design decisions (indexes, query shape, concurrency rules) stay with you, and EF Core gives you the tools to express them.

steps.title: DbContext and DbSet
body: Two types carry most of EF Core:
- **`DbContext`** is your session with the database. You write a class that derives from it, and that class says which database to use and which tables exist.
- **`DbSet<T>`** is one table, seen as a collection of `T`. You query it with LINQ and add to it like a list.
```csharp fragment
class LibraryDb : DbContext
public DbSet<Book> Books => Set<Book>();       // the Books table
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options)
=> options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db");   // which database

`UseSqlite` picks the **provider**: the part of EF Core that speaks one database's dialect of SQL. SQLite keeps the whole database in one file (`library.db`). The same code runs against SQL Server or PostgreSQL by swapping the provider.
> **Tip:** In this course every program runs in its own fresh folder, so `library.db` always starts out missing.

steps.prompt: Complete the context so it has a `Books` table and uses SQLite.
steps.explain: The context derives from `DbContext`, each table is a `DbSet<T>`, and `UseSqlite` chooses the SQLite provider.

steps.title: A whole program
body: Here is everything together. Read it top to bottom: create the context, make sure the database exists, add a book, save, then query.
```csharp fragment
using var db = new LibraryDb();
db.Database.EnsureCreated();          // creates library.db and its tables if missing
db.Books.Add(new Book { Title = "Dune", Year = 1965 });
db.SaveChanges();                     // runs the INSERT
foreach (var b in db.Books.OrderBy(b => b.Year))
Console.WriteLine($"{b.Id}: {b.Title} ({b.Year})");
Three things to notice:
- `Add` does **not** touch the database. It only tells the context "this object is new". `SaveChanges` sends the SQL.
- `Id` was never set, yet it prints `1`. The database generated it, and EF Core copied it back into the object.
- `db.Books.OrderBy(...)` is not a loop over a list in memory. It becomes `SELECT ... ORDER BY "Year"` and runs in the database.

steps.explain: `db.Books.Count()` is a query: it asks the database. Before `SaveChanges` nothing has been inserted, so the table is empty. After it, both rows exist.
hints: Does `Add` write to the database, or does `SaveChanges`?

steps.prompt: You call `db.Books.Add(book)` and the program ends without calling `SaveChanges`. What is in the database?
options: Nothing new: the book was only tracked in memory
Half a row, with only the `Id` column
An error is thrown when the program ends
steps.explain: `Add` marks the object as *Added* in the context. Only `SaveChanges` turns that into an `INSERT`. Drop the context without saving and the change is simply forgotten.

steps.title: Your first table
prompt: - `Movie` with an `int Id`, a `string Title` (default `""`) and an `int Minutes`.
- `CinemaDb`, a `DbContext` with a `DbSet<Movie>` called `Movies`, using SQLite with `Data Source=cinema.db`.
The tests create the database, add two movies, save, and read them back with a new context. **Run checks** to try it.
starter: // a Movies table, and OnConfiguring with UseSqlite
template: Dojo.Check("EnsureCreated creates the database", dojoDb.Database.EnsureCreated(), "EnsureCreated returned false: was the database already there?");
var dojoAll = dojoDb.Movies.OrderBy(m => m.Id).Select(m => m.Title + " " + m.Minutes).ToList();
Dojo.Eq("a new context reads them back", new List<string> { "Alien 117", "Up 96" }, dojoAll);
Dojo.Eq("ids were generated", new List<int> { 1, 2 }, dojoDb.Movies.OrderBy(m => m.Id).Select(m => m.Id).ToList());
Dojo.Check("uses the file cinema.db", File.Exists("cinema.db"), "no cinema.db was created next to the program");
hints: A table is `public DbSet<Movie> Movies => Set<Movie>();`
Copy the shape of `LibraryDb` from the lesson, changing the names.
